name: ATD (1,4,6-androstatrienedione)
lead: ATD (1,4,6-androstatriene-3,17-dione) is a steroid-type compound described as an irreversible aromatase inhibitor: it binds the enzyme that converts androgens such as testosterone into estrogens and permanently inactivates it in fat and other peripheral tissue [1][2]. People in muscle-building circles took it to hold down estrogen conversion, with the aim of keeping a drier, leaner look and avoiding estrogen-related effects such as gynecomastia, which they associated with a better-looking physique [2][4].

It was sold over the counter in bodybuilding supplements, reportedly until 2009, in oral and topical forms and under many alternative names, and a T Nation poster describes it as a product still seen for sale and as a metabolite of boldenone [1][4]. Wikipedia credits supplement-industry figure Bruce Kneller with developing and commercialising it, and links the product to Gaspari Nutrition [1].

Published work consists of laboratory enzyme studies and an animal study; no human trial of ATD for body composition, gynecomastia or any other appearance outcome has been identified. It is prohibited in sports that ban aromatase inhibitors [1].

paras: ATD is described as binding aromatase and permanently inactivating it in fat and other peripheral tissue, which lowers estrogen production [1]. A 1981 study cited by Wikipedia described enzyme-generated intermediates that progressively reduce placental aromatase activity [1]. A 1995 chemistry paper evaluated 4-thio-substituted derivatives of 1,4,6-androstatrienedione and related dienediones and reported potent inhibition of aromatase in human placental microsomes [3].

Aromatase inhibitors as a class are divided into irreversible steroidal types, such as exemestane, and reversible nonsteroidal types, such as anastrozole and letrozole [2]. Wikipedia lists reported effects of the class including reduced bone maturation, hair loss and liver dysfunction, and notes that they are used in men for hormone-sensitive cancers and sometimes off-label to manage estrogen during testosterone therapy [2]. These class effects were not measured for ATD itself.

ATD appeared in some over-the-counter supplements until 2009, and topical products were also marketed [1]. Wikipedia credits supplement-industry figure Bruce Kneller with developing and commercialising it and notes he holds a related US patent [1]. Sellers used many alternative names, which can make products harder to identify [1].

ATD is prohibited in amateur and professional sport as an aromatase inhibitor. It is also reported that ATD can produce a positive test for the anabolic steroid boldenone, of which it is a possible metabolite and manufacturing contaminant [1].
A 2009 paper cited by Wikipedia examined ATD metabolism and its detection by GC/MS in doping control [1]. ATD can be made from DHEA in a single oxidation step [1].

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: On T Nation, a poster advising another lifter points to ATD (arimistane) as a suicidal aromatase inhibitor and a boldenone metabolite that could still be bought over the counter [4]. Searches of the forum for the abbreviation also return unrelated content, since the same letters name other things.

No studies found. A 1984 study in rhesus monkeys, cited by Wikipedia, reported that aromatase inhibition increased luteinizing hormone and testosterone secretion; this was animal research and not a test of appearance outcomes [1].

timeline.event: Study describes enzyme-generated intermediates of ATD that progressively reduce placental aromatase activity [1].
Rhesus monkey study reports raised LH and testosterone with aromatase inhibition [1].
Paper reports 4-thio derivatives of 1,4,6-androstatrienedione as potent aromatase inhibitors in vitro [3].
Approximate end of ATD's presence in over-the-counter supplements [1].

lore.intro: ATD appears in muscle-building forums as an over-the-counter aromatase inhibitor, usually mentioned in passing in advice to other lifters [4].

claims.claim: ATD lowers estrogen so users stay lean and avoid gynecomastia
claims.believers: A T Nation poster recommends looking up ATD as a suicidal aromatase inhibitor for someone trying to control estrogen [4].
claims.experts: Reference texts describe irreversible aromatase inhibition in enzyme studies, and a rhesus monkey study reported raised LH and testosterone with aromatase inhibition; no human trial of ATD has reported appearance outcomes [1].

claims.claim: ATD is a legal over-the-counter option
claims.believers: The same poster believes it can still be bought over the counter [4].
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists the US status as supplement and says ATD appeared in OTC supplements until 2009; it is prohibited in sports banning aromatase inhibitors and may cause a boldenone-positive test [1].

card.summary: A prohormone-era supplement aromatase inhibitor with lab data behind its mechanism and no human trials behind any look-related claim.
card.note: Banned in sport; can trigger a boldenone-positive drug test.

quick.overview:
ATD is a steroid-like supplement ingredient that was sold over the counter in the prohormone era, reportedly until around 2009. It is described as an aromatase inhibitor, which in theory lowers estrogen.

Its discussion in muscle-building communities centres on controlling estrogen. No human trial of its effects on muscle, gynecomastia or appearance was found.
quick.mechanism: Described as an irreversible aromatase inhibitor: it binds the enzyme that makes estrogen from androgens and inactivates it. Evidence is from enzyme studies and an old monkey study.
quick.risks: No human safety data were found. It is banned in sport and can reportedly cause a positive boldenone test. Products sold under varied names can be hard to identify.

chain: Less conversion of testosterone to estrogen
Claimed: leaner look, less estrogen-related fat or breast tissue
angle.text: Users took ATD to lower estrogen conversion, expecting a leaner, harder look and protection against gynecomastia while using other prohormones or androgens. This is the reasoning described by proponents; it has not been tested in human trials of ATD.
